title: Bible Study Stop Sign
subject: Criminal Law & Procedure
stem:
After learning that he had lost his job as a private bar-prep tutor, Peter stayed late at a wedding reception hosted by friends from his Bible study and drank heavily. While driving home, Peter noticed headlights behind him and, in his intoxicated state, concluded that robbers from the parking lot were following him. In fact, Officer John was following Peter on suspicion of drunk driving. In his effort to get away, Peter sped through a stop sign and struck and killed Ruth, who was crossing the street. Peter was arrested.

Peter is prosecuted for manslaughter. Peter should be
call: Peter is prosecuted for manslaughter. Peter should be

choices.A: acquitted, because he honestly believed he faced an imminent threat of death or severe bodily injury.
choices.B: acquitted, because his intoxication prevented him from appreciating the risk he created.
choices.C: convicted, because he acted recklessly and in fact was in no danger.
choices.D: convicted, because he acted recklessly and his apprehension of danger was not reasonable.

rightExplanation:
D is correct because Peter caused a death while driving recklessly, and neither asserted defense gets him out.

Gold Key: Voluntary intoxication does not erase recklessness. A defendant who would have appreciated the risk when sober is treated as reckless even if his drunkenness kept him from actually appreciating it.

Gold Key: In this trap, do not ask whether danger actually existed. Ask whether the defendant’s apprehension of danger was reasonable enough to support self-defense against a recklessness-based manslaughter charge.

Silver Key: C and D both convict Peter because he acted recklessly. The C/D fight is not “convict or acquit.” It is actual danger versus reasonable apprehension. D names the legally decisive axis.

wrongExplanations.A: It gives Peter too much credit for an honest fear. Honest fear alone is not enough on this answer set. The missing word is reasonable. The answer is a half-truth.
wrongExplanations.B: Gold Key: Voluntary intoxication does not make recklessness disappear. This answer runs the intoxication rule in the wrong direction.
wrongExplanations.C: Silver Key: C picks the wrong fact inside the correct conviction result. The problem is not that Peter was “in fact” safe. A person can sometimes defend based on a reasonable mistaken belief. The defect here is that Peter’s apprehension was not reasonable.

c3.label: CUT A
c3.text: “Honestly believed” is incomplete. It omits the reasonableness requirement. This is anchor-assisted, not pure structure.

c3.label: CUT B
c3.text: “Intoxication prevented appreciation” reverses the recklessness-intoxication rule. This is anchor-assisted.

c3.label: CLASH C vs. D
c3.text: Both convict. Both say reckless. The axis is actual danger versus reasonable apprehension.

c3.label: CALL/Anchor
c3.text: The Gold Key resolves the axis. Actual danger is not the required fact. Reasonable apprehension is. D survives.

studentScript: Manslaughter charge. Death from reckless flight. A only gives honest fear. B says intoxication erases risk awareness; Gold Key says no. C and D both convict; the fight is no actual danger versus unreasonable apprehension. Actual danger is the wrong axis. D.

A.signal: The choice gives only honest fear. The array is asking whether that fear legally excuses reckless manslaughter.
A.lawyer: Self-defense needs more than an honest fear on this answer set; the belief/apprehension must satisfy the governing reasonableness or MPC recklessness limitation.

B.signal: The answer says intoxication blocks recklessness. The Gold Key says voluntary intoxication does not erase recklessness.
B.lawyer: Under MPC intoxication treatment, self-induced intoxication does not excuse recklessness where sober awareness would exist.

C.signal: C says the important fact is that Peter was in no actual danger. The C/D pair fights over actual danger versus reasonable apprehension.
C.lawyer: A reasonable mistaken belief can sometimes support self-defense; the defect here is unreasonable apprehension, not merely absence of actual danger.

D.signal: D keeps the correct conviction result and names the responsive reason: reckless conduct plus unreasonable apprehension.
D.lawyer: Peter recklessly caused a death; voluntary intoxication does not excuse the risk, and his unreasonable danger belief does not supply a valid self-defense.

goldKeys.statement: Voluntary intoxication does not erase recklessness. If the defendant would have perceived the risk when sober, the law treats him as reckless even if drunkenness kept him from seeing it.
goldKeys.trigger: manslaughter or reckless crime plus voluntary intoxication plus claim of not appreciating risk
goldKeys.unlocks: Choice B and the intoxication defense trap

goldKeys.statement: In a self-defense manslaughter trap, do not ask only whether the defendant honestly feared danger or whether danger actually existed. Ask whether the apprehension was reasonable enough to excuse the reckless killing.
goldKeys.trigger: honest fear / no actual danger / apprehension not reasonable answer set

silverKeys.statement: When two answers both convict because the defendant acted recklessly, stop comparing outcomes. The fight is actual danger versus reasonable apprehension.
silverKeys.trigger: two conviction answers, both using recklessness, with one saying no actual danger and the other saying apprehension not reasonable

remediation.title: Reckless homicide: defense axis check
remediation.studentMove: Cut intoxication-as-no-risk; then clash actual danger against reasonable apprehension.
remediation.tinyRule: Recklessness survives voluntary intoxication; self-defense turns on reasonable apprehension, not actual danger alone.
remediation.trap: Picking C because it states the true fact that there was no actual danger.
